name: The Four Kinds of Arthropod
scope: The most successful body plan on Earth splits by leg count and habit: insects (6 legs, 3 body parts), arachnids (8 legs — spiders, scorpions, ticks), crustaceans (mostly aquatic — crabs, lobsters, shrimp), and myriapods (centipedes and millipedes, many legs). Count the legs to name the group.
source: Britannica; AMNH invertebrate zoology
framing_note: Leg-count as the sorting handle — a spider isn't an insect because it has 8 legs. Scene-led. Distractors put a spider in with insects, a centipede with crustaceans.

name: Seeing With Sound (echolocation)
scope: Bats and dolphins map the dark by shouting and listening to the echoes — a bat can pinpoint a mosquito in total blackness, a dolphin can 'see' a fish buried in sand. The bat screams so loudly it must briefly deafen its own ears to avoid harming itself between calls.
source: Britannica; Donald Griffin (coined 'echolocation'); AMNH
framing_note: The bat-must-deafen-itself and dolphin-sees-through-sand facts are the payoffs. Scene-led (hunting in total dark). Distractors: attribute echolocation to owls (they use hearing but not echolocation).

name: The Mantis Shrimp's Eyes
scope: The mantis shrimp has 16 types of color receptor to a human's 3, plus the ability to see polarized and circular-polarized light — the only animals known to do so. But the twist (2014, Thoen & Marshall) is that they're actually POOR at telling similar colors apart: instead of comparing signals like us, they seem to use a fast scanning recognition system that's still being studied.
source: Thoen, How, Chiou & Marshall 2014 (Science, 'A Different Form of Color Vision'); Cronin/Marshall stomatopod reviews
framing_note: MANDATORY accuracy caution: do NOT claim mantis shrimp 'see more colors' as fact — the research overturned that. The genuine wonder is the paradox (16 receptors yet poor discrimination; a recognition-not-comparison system that is research-in-progress). Frame the correction itself as the payoff. Scene-led.

name: The Octopus
scope: The keystone alien-on-Earth ladder: three hearts (two pump the gills, one the body; the body heart stops when it swims, so it prefers crawling); blue copper-based blood; a distributed 'nine brains' nervous system with two-thirds of neurons in the arms, so a severed arm can still grab; opens jars and hunts by touch; changes color with chromatophores/iridophores/leucophores while being colorblind (it may sense color through its skin); the coconut octopus carries shell halves as portable armor (first documented invertebrate tool use); the mimic octopus impersonates 15+ species.
source: Britannica; AMNH; MBARI; Godfrey-Smith 'Other Minds'; Finn et al. 2009 (coconut octopus)
framing_note: The bank's marquee wonder ladder — one deep story, one fact per rung, T2 (three hearts) climbing to T5 (colorblind-yet-camouflaging paradox, skin-based light sensing which is research-in-progress). No anthropomorphizing intelligence as human thought; describe behaviors (solves, opens, mimics). Real binomials only. Absorbs cephalopod_intelligence, tool_use_octopus, octopus_camouflage.

name: The Egg-Laying Mammals (Monotremes)
scope: Only five living species break the mammal rules: the platypus and four echidna species lay eggs yet still make milk. No nipples — milk oozes through patches of skin. The platypus also has a venomous spur and a duck bill that senses electricity.
source: Britannica; Australian Museum; AMNH
framing_note: Wonder-led: the platypus is a rule-breaking mash-up (bill, spur, eggs, milk-through-skin). Real binomial Ornithorhynchus anatinus if named. Only 5 living monotreme species — state exactly. No anthropomorphizing.

name: The Five Vertebrate Classes
scope: The backbone family portrait: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals. Each rung sorts a harvested creature into its class by the one give-away trait (feathers = bird, fur + milk = mammal, scales + cold-blooded = reptile, wet skin + tadpole youth = amphibian, gills = fish). Top rung: birds ARE living theropod dinosaurs, so the 'five classes' hides a dinosaur among them.
source: Britannica; AMNH vertebrate overview
framing_note: Scene-led recognition: a kid names what they just skinned by its tell, not by memorizing a definition. Avoid 'What is a mammal?' shells; each rung leads with a concrete animal or trait. Keep taxonomy current (birds nested inside reptiles cladistically; note plainly at top tier without turning it into a lecture).

name: The Axolotl
scope: A Mexican salamander that never grows up — it keeps its feathery gills and stays aquatic for life (neoteny) instead of turning into a land salamander. Its superpower is regeneration: it regrows whole limbs, parts of its heart, and even portions of its brain and spinal cord, scar-free. Nearly extinct in the wild (Lake Xochimilco) yet common in labs and aquariums.
source: Britannica; AMNH; regeneration research (e.g. Tanaka lab); IUCN (wild status)
framing_note: The regrows-its-own-brain fact is the payoff; neoteny (a 'Peter Pan' salamander) is the concrete handle. Scene-led. Note the wild-vs-lab paradox honestly. Real species Ambystoma mexicanum if named.

name: The Blue Whale (the largest ever)
scope: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived — bigger than any dinosaur — reaching about 30 m and up to ~200 tonnes. Its tongue alone can weigh as much as an elephant, its heart is the size of a small car, and a newborn calf gains around 90 kg (200 lb) a day on its mother's milk.
source: Britannica; NOAA Fisheries; AMNH
framing_note: T1 anchor (largest animal alive today / ever) climbing to vivid comparisons (tongue = an elephant; heart = a car; calf gains 200 lb/day). Numbers work as built-up payoffs. Scene-led. 'Bigger than any dinosaur' is accurate and a strong hook.

name: The Coelacanth: A Fish From the Age of Dinosaurs
scope: In 1938 a museum curator, Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, recognized an ugly blue fish in a South African trawler's catch as something thought extinct for 66 million years - a coelacanth, a lobe-finned fish close to the ancestors of land animals. It has fleshy limb-like fins, gives live birth, and a hinged skull found nowhere else alive today.
source: Britannica; coelacanth (Latimeria) discovery (Courtenay-Latimer, Smith 1939); Latimeria biology
framing_note: The 'a living fossil hauled up from a fishing boat by someone who recognized it' story is the payoff; the lobe fins connect to the tetrapod-origins theme (Pillar 2) but stays about the living animal. Scene-led. Real genus Latimeria. Factual - not literally unchanged, but a deep relict lineage.

name: The Electric Eel
scope: Not a true eel but a South American knifefish that turns its body into a living battery: thousands of stacked electric cells fire together for a jolt up to 860 volts (the record, measured in Electrophorus voltai, one of three species named only in 2019 — named for Alessandro Volta, whose battery it inspired). It stuns prey, can leap to press its shock onto a threat, and navigates with weak electric pulses.
source: de Santana et al. 2019 (electric eel = 3 species; E. voltai 860V, Nature Communications); Kenneth Catania (leaping-attack studies)
framing_note: The 860V record and the Volta-battery naming are the payoffs (number built up as punchline). Accuracy: it's a knifefish, NOT a true eel; 860V belongs to E. voltai specifically; the 3-species split dates to 2019. Real binomials only. Absorbs electric_eel_voltage + electric_eel_shock.

name: The Immortal Jellyfish
scope: Turritopsis dohrnii, a jellyfish the size of a pinky nail, can cheat death: when injured, starving, or old, its adult body reverts all the way back to its juvenile polyp stage and starts life over — like a butterfly turning back into a caterpillar. In principle this cycle can repeat forever, so it's called 'biologically immortal' (though predators and disease still kill it).
source: Britannica; Piraino et al. 1996 (transdifferentiation); Smithsonian Ocean
framing_note: The butterfly-back-to-caterpillar handle makes 'transdifferentiation' concrete. Accuracy: 'immortal' means it can escape aging, NOT that it can't be killed — state the caveat. Real binomial Turritopsis dohrnii. Scene-led.

name: The Mantis Shrimp's Punch
scope: The smasher mantis shrimp throws the fastest punch in the sea: its spring-loaded club accelerates like a .22 bullet, striking so fast it boils the water into imploding cavitation bubbles that flash with light and heat — a second shockwave that hits even if the first strike misses. It can crack aquarium glass and shatter crab shells.
source: Sheila Patek (mantis shrimp strike biomechanics, Nature 2004); Britannica
framing_note: The bullet-fast, water-boiling, twice-hitting punch is pure dinner-table wonder — build the cavitation as a payoff. Scene-led (cracking aquarium glass). Pair with the separate eyes ladder but keep this one about the strike. Factual biomechanics.

name: The Naked Mole-Rat
scope: A wrinkled, nearly hairless, buck-toothed rodent that breaks the rules of mammal life: it lives in an insect-like colony ruled by a single breeding queen (eusocial, like ants), survives ~30 years when a mouse gets ~3, almost never gets cancer, feels no pain from acid or chili burns, and can go minutes with almost no oxygen by burning fructose like a plant.
source: Britannica; Buffenstein lab (longevity/cancer resistance); Park et al. 2017 (fructose metabolism, Science)
framing_note: A keystone weird-mammal ladder — each rung is one rule it breaks (queen, 30-year lifespan, cancer resistance, pain insensitivity, oxygen-free survival). Scene-led. All facts documented; no exaggeration ('almost never' not 'never' for cancer). Real, wondrous, factual.

name: The Tardigrade (water bear)
scope: A half-millimeter eight-legged 'water bear' that is nearly indestructible: by curling into a dried-out 'tun' (cryptobiosis) it survives boiling, freezing near absolute zero, crushing pressure, blasts of radiation, and even the raw vacuum of open space — tardigrades were exposed to space on a 2007 orbital mission and lived.
source: Britannica; Jönsson et al. 2008 (TARDIS space-exposure experiment); AMNH
framing_note: The 'survived open space' fact is the marquee payoff; each rung stacks one extreme it survives. Scene-led. Keep 'nearly indestructible' honest (they die eventually; cryptobiosis is the mechanism). Real, wondrous, factual.

name: Mary Anning
scope: Self-taught and poor, struck by lightning as a baby and surviving it, Mary Anning combed the crumbling cliffs of Lyme Regis for a living and found deep time itself: the first ichthyosaur (age 12, 1811), the first complete plesiosaur (1823), the first British pterosaur (1828) — yet as a woman was barred from the scientific societies that used her finds.
source: NHM London (Mary Anning); Britannica; Lyme Regis Museum; Anning biographies
framing_note: Keystone human ladder — the poverty, the self-teaching, the lightning survival, and the named firsts (ichthyosaur/plesiosaur/pterosaur) are all payoffs; the exclusion-as-a-woman is the moral throughline. Standard science; real dates. Named finds over years.

name: The Bone Wars (Cope vs. Marsh)
scope: Two rich rivals, Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh, spent the 1870s-90s racing to out-dig each other across the American West — bribing, spying, dynamiting sites so the other couldn't have them, and naming ~130 new dinosaurs (Triceratops, Stegosaurus, Allosaurus) while bankrupting and disgracing themselves. Marsh even put the wrong head on 'Brontosaurus'.
source: Britannica; NHM records; Bone Wars histories (Wallace, 'The Bonehunters' Revenge')
framing_note: Keystone story ladder — the sabotage, dynamiting, and the wrong-head-on-Brontosaurus are the dinner-table payoffs; name Cope and Marsh as the antagonists. Standard science; the dinosaurs they named are real. Named feud over dates.

name: Lucy the Australopithecus
scope: In 1974 at Hadar, Ethiopia, Donald Johanson found ~40% of a 3.2-million-year-old skeleton — Australopithecus afarensis — proving our ancestors walked upright long before big brains evolved. The team named her Lucy because the Beatles' 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds' was playing at camp that night.
source: Britannica; Institute of Human Origins; Johanson 'Lucy'; NHM records
framing_note: Base T2 rung delivers the Beatles-song naming (pure dinner-table gold); climb to bipedalism-before-big-brains. Standard science stated confidently. Named fossil and the Beatles story over the date.

name: Neanderthals
scope: Not brutish cavemen but skilled cold-adapted humans — Neanderthals buried their dead, made tools and pigments, cared for the injured, had bigger brains than us, and vanished ~40,000 years ago. The twist: they didn't fully die out — most people alive outside Africa carry ~2% Neanderthal DNA.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Pääbo Neanderthal genome; Reich lab introgression studies
framing_note: Bust the 'dumb caveman' myth, then land the '2% of your DNA is Neanderthal' payoff. Standard science stated confidently; the interbreeding is settled. Named species and the DNA fact over the extinction date.

name: Whales Walked on Land (Pakicetus)
scope: The blue whale's ancestor had legs and lived on land — Pakicetus (~50M, dog-sized, hoofed) walked riverbanks in Pakistan, then Ambulocetus ('walking whale') took to the water, Rodhocetus's legs shrank, and the fossil series shows the whole march from shore to sea; whales still have vestigial hip bones.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Thewissen / Gingerich cetacean-transition literature
framing_note: Keystone transitional ladder — the named intermediates (Pakicetus, Ambulocetus, Rodhocetus) and the vestigial hip bones are the payoffs. Standard science stated confidently: whales descended from land mammals, one of the best-documented transitions.

name: Smilodon, the Sabertooth Cat
scope: The saber-toothed cat — Smilodon, with 18cm canines and a bear-like muscular build, killed with a precise throat bite (the fragile fangs couldn't take struggling prey). Deep ladder anchored on La Brea: thousands died trapped in the tar, and healed injuries in the bones hint they lived in social groups that cared for the hurt.
source: Britannica; La Brea Tar Pits / Page Museum; Smilodon paleobiology literature
framing_note: Base T2 gives the icon; climb to the throat-bite mechanics and La Brea social-behavior inference. Standard science; note 'sabertooth' is convergent — Smilodon is a true cat, unlike the Permian gorgonopsians. Named cat over the 18cm number.

name: The Woolly Mammoth
scope: The Ice Age icon — Mammuthus primigenius, curved 4m tusks, a fatty hump, found frozen with skin and stomach contents in Siberian permafrost. Deep ladder: the grazing giant, the frozen 'ice mummies', and the stunner that a holdout population survived on Wrangel Island until ~4,000 years ago — after the Great Pyramid was built.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Wrangel Island mammoth-survival literature
framing_note: Base T2 rung gives the iconic tusked grazer; climb to the Wrangel-outlived-the-pyramids gut-punch. Standard science; correct genus (Mammuthus). The 'younger than the pyramids' fact is the killer retell — constructed, not a cold date.

name: Tyrannosaurus rex
scope: Late Cretaceous (68-66M) North America's apex predator — ~12m, banana-sized serrated teeth, a bite that could crush bone (the strongest of any land animal ever), forward-facing eyes for binocular vision, and tiny but powerfully muscled arms. Deep ladder from the base fact up to bite-force and growth science.
source: Britannica; NHM London; AMNH; T. rex bite-force / growth-curve studies
framing_note: Base T2 rungs give the iconic predator; climb to bone-crushing bite force and binocular vision. ALWAYS 'T. rex' or 'Tyrannosaurus rex' — never 'T. Rex'. Standard science; feathers on tyrannosaurs are debated, so hedge honestly rather than asserting.

name: The Day the Dinosaurs Died (K-Pg / Chicxulub)
scope: 66M years ago a 10-km asteroid slammed into the Yucatán at Chicxulub, ending the non-avian dinosaurs. Deep ladder: Walter & Luis Alvarez's 1980 iridium-layer clue (metal from space in a global clay band), the 1991 crater confirmation, the ~180km crater buried under Mexico, the impact winter, and that BIRDS are the dinosaurs that survived.
source: Britannica; Alvarez et al. 1980 Science; NHM London; Chicxulub crater literature
framing_note: Keystone ladder — include accessible T2 base rungs (asteroid hit the dinosaurs) climbing to the Alvarez iridium detective story at T4-T5. Standard science stated confidently; birds ARE surviving theropod dinosaurs. Named things (Chicxulub, the iridium layer, the Alvarezes) beat dates.

name: Milk Across Species
scope: Cow, goat, sheep, water buffalo (Indian dairy backbone + mozzarella di bufala), yak (Himalayan), camel, horse (mare's-milk airag/kumis) and reindeer all milked; goat milk's smaller fat globules (easier digestion, pH nearer human milk); sheep milk highest fat (~7% vs. cow ~3.5%, base of Roquefort/Pecorino/feta); camel milk's lower lactose and insulin-like protein researched for diabetics.
source: Britannica; FAO dairy species data; Park (2007) minor-species milk composition
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the milk with the highest fat, curdled into Roquefort' → sheep; 'the low-lactose desert milk researched for diabetics' → camel. Named cheeses and species are the handles. Camel-milk diabetic claim framed as researched, not proven. No policy drift.

name: Cattle: Aurochs to Three Origins
scope: ~10,500 BP; wild aurochs (Bos primigenius) as ancestor; independent taurine (Near East, Bos taurus) and zebu (Indian subcontinent, Bos indicus) domestications plus a distinct African line; the aurochs' 1627 extinction (last cow in Poland's Jaktorow Forest); humped vs. humpless split; the small founding herd (~80 females, genetics suggest).
source: Britannica; Zeder; Bollongino (2012) cattle-founder genetics; aurochs extinction record (Jaktorow 1627)
framing_note: Scene-led: the towering wild aurochs behind every modern cow, extinct in a Polish royal forest. Named ancestor and place beat generic 'origin'. No policy drift.

name: Sheep & Goat: Fertile Crescent Firsts
scope: ~11,000 BP domestication in the Fertile Crescent; mouflon (Ovis) → sheep and bezoar ibex (Capra) → goat; among the very first agricultural domesticates alongside grain; the shift from hunting to herding; the secondary-products revolution (wool/milk after meat); why goats browse and sheep graze.
source: Britannica; Zeder domestication archaeology; The Livestock Conservancy
framing_note: Scene-led: the first herders of the Zagros foothills, wild mouflon in the hills. Concrete wild-ancestor names beat 'first livestock'. No policy drift.

name: The Dog: First Domesticate
scope: The gray wolf (Canis lupus) as ancestor of every dog; the ~15,000-40,000 BP domestication window (oldest of all); the single-vs-multiple-origin debate; the human-camp scavenging pathway; how commensal wolves diverged behaviorally before morphologically; the Bonn-Oberkassel dog burial (~14,000 BP) as early companionship evidence.
source: Britannica; Larson & Bradley (2014, PLOS Genetics) dog-origins review; Freedman & Wayne genome studies; Bonn-Oberkassel burial
framing_note: Scene-led: a wolf drawn to the warmth of a human fire, not 'what animal did dogs descend from?'. Practical anchor: this is the ur-story of husbandry the harvester should know. Present single-vs-multiple-origin as a live scientific debate, not a settled verdict.

name: The Horse: Botai Revolution
scope: ~5,500 BP Botai culture, Kazakhstan (bit wear on teeth, mare's-milk residue in pots); how the horse transformed transport, trade and warfare; the later discovery that Botai horses were Przewalski ancestors, not the source of modern domestic horses (2018 genetics twist); the true modern-horse origin traced to the Western Steppe (~4,200 BP).
source: Outram (2009) Botai study; Gaunitz (2018, Science) Przewalski reassignment; Librado (2021, Nature) horse-origins; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: milk-residue pots and bit-worn teeth on the Kazakh steppe. The 2018/2021 twists (Botai not the modern ancestor; true origin on the Western Steppe) are memorable upper-tier reveals. Present as evolving science. No policy drift.

name: Venison Field Dressing
scope: The moment after the kill decides whether the meat is good: gut the deer within the hour to shed body heat, keep the punctured stomach and gut bacteria off the flesh, and let air reach the body cavity. Avoid the scent glands (tarsal glands on the hind legs) and don't taint the meat. Cool it fast, hang and age it 7-14 days at just above freezing, then quarter it to pack out. Backstrap and tenderloin are the tender prizes along the spine.
source: Britannica; state hunter-education field-dressing guides; MeatEater butchery references
framing_note: Directly practical — this is the player's harvest action. No-waste and quick-handling framed as the actual skill hunters practice, not preaching. Named prizes (backstrap, tenderloin) and pitfalls (tarsal glands) as answers. Hunting legitimate; no advocacy.

name: Beef Primal Cuts
scope: The eight US primals mapped onto the steer: chuck (shoulder, pot roasts and the chuck-eye), rib (ribeye, prime rib), short loin (the tender strip, T-bone, filet mignon from the tenderloin), sirloin and round (rear, lean roasts), brisket (breast, low-and-slow for barbecue), plate (skirt steak), flank (flank steak), and shank (shin, for stock). The rule the player can use: muscles that work hard (chuck, round, shank, brisket) are tough and want slow moist heat; the barely-used loin and rib are tender and take fast dry heat.
source: Britannica; USDA/NAMP beef cut charts; 'On Food and Cooking' (McGee)
framing_note: Practical anchoring — the player butchers in-game, so where a cut sits and what it yields has real value. Answer = the named cut (ribeye, brisket, filet mignon, skirt), not a generic label. The 'hard-working muscle = tough, slow-cook' principle is the load-bearing teaching. No stance issues.

name: Pork Primal Cuts
scope: The hog broken down: shoulder (Boston butt and picnic — pulled pork), loin (chops, tenderloin, back ribs, and the cured loin that becomes Canadian bacon), belly (bacon, fresh-side, pancetta), ham (the hind leg, cured or fresh), spareribs from the belly and baby-backs from the loin, and the jowl (guanciale). The 'butt' is confusingly from the FRONT shoulder, not the rear — named for the barrels (butts) it was once packed in.
source: Britannica; USDA pork cut charts; National Pork Board
framing_note: Practical, player uses it. The Boston-butt-is-the-shoulder trap (and the barrel etymology) and the belly-to-bacon fact are memorable payoffs (named things over labels). No stance issues.

name: The American Bison's Near-Extinction
scope: Perhaps 30 million bison thundered across the plains before 1800; hide hunters with long-range Sharps rifles and the railroads that shipped the hides dropped the count below 1,000 wild animals by 1889. Tongues and hides were taken and carcasses left to rot on the prairie, the bones later gathered for fertilizer; the collapse also devastated the Plains nations who lived on the herds. Careful recovery — from a handful of private and Yellowstone survivors — has since rebuilt them to roughly half a million.
source: Britannica; Smithsonian; American Bison Society history
framing_note: The bridge topic: near-extinction AND restoration in one animal. Keep it about the ANIMAL and the vivid slaughter/recovery (Sharps rifle, bone-pickers, the Yellowstone remnant), not the laws. The wasteful hide-only kill sharpens the no-waste ethic by contrast. Plainly told, weighty.

name: The Dodo
scope: A flightless, fearless pigeon relative found only on Mauritius, taller than a turkey with a great hooked bill. Dutch sailors clubbed them for meat while their dogs, pigs, monkeys, and rats ate the ground-laid eggs. Barely 80 years passed from European discovery (1598) to the last sighting (~1662); no complete specimen survives, only paintings, scattered bones, and one dried head and foot at Oxford. Its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon.
source: Britannica; Natural History Museum (London); Oxford University Museum of Natural History
framing_note: The extinction stated plainly and with weight — honest history, no 'humans bad' staging. Answer = named things (the dodo, the Oxford head) and vivid actions (the pigs eating the eggs). The Nicobar-pigeon relative is a strong T4 payoff.

name: The Great Auk
scope: A flightless, penguin-like seabird of the North Atlantic (it was the ORIGINAL 'penguin'), hunted for meat, eggs, oil, and its dense down. As it grew rare, collectors made it worse — museums paid ever more for the last specimens. The final pair was strangled on the Icelandic islet of Eldey on June 3, 1844, and the single egg they were incubating was crushed underfoot.
source: Britannica; Errol Fuller, 'The Great Auk'; Smithsonian
framing_note: Plainly told, weighty. The crushed egg and the named islet (Eldey) are the memorable handles; the 'original penguin' name-transfer is a strong payoff. The grim irony: collecting for museums finished the job. No advocacy.

name: The Passenger Pigeon and Martha
scope: Once the most abundant bird in North America — flocks of billions that darkened the sky for days as they passed, breaking tree limbs where they roosted. Market hunters shipped them by the boxcar to city tables; telegraph and railroad let gunners find every nesting colony, and the birds needed dense colonies to breed. The species collapsed within decades, and the very last one, a hen named Martha, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914.
source: Britannica; Smithsonian (Martha specimen); Cincinnati Zoo history; A.W. Schorger population studies
framing_note: The pillar's flagship extinction ladder. Stated plainly, real weight, no staging. Answer hierarchy: named things (Martha, Cincinnati Zoo) and the sky-darkening image over any number. Both barrels of overhunting AND habitat loss (deforested nesting grounds); the colony-breeding collapse is the T5 wonder rung.

name: The Thylacine (Tasmanian Tiger)
scope: A striped, wolf-like marsupial that could open its jaws to a startling 80 degrees and carried young in a backward-facing pouch (present in BOTH sexes). Blamed — largely wrongly — for killing sheep, it was hunted under a government bounty of one pound per head. The last known one, later called Benjamin, died of exposure at Hobart's Beaumaris Zoo in 1936, locked out of its shelter on a freezing night; grainy black-and-white film of it survives, and reported sightings still trickle in.
source: Britannica; National Museum of Australia; Australian Museum
framing_note: Plainly told, weighty; note the sheep-killing reputation was mostly a false charge that fueled the bounty. Answer = named things (thylacine, Benjamin) and vivid biology (80-degree gape, backward pouch in both sexes). The surviving film and lingering sightings are the T5 wonder rungs. No advocacy.

name: Indigenous Whaling and Hunting Rights
scope: When a people has hunted an animal for millennia, does a modern ban override their treaty and cultural right? The Makah of Washington killed a gray whale in 1999 under an 1855 treaty right — the first in over 70 years — drawing protest and years of court battles; Alaskan Inuit hunt bowheads under subsistence quotas from the whale-boat captain (umialik); the Faroese grindadrap drives pilot whales into a bay to be killed communally, condemned abroad as cruel and defended as sustainable traditional food. Cultural continuity and food sovereignty on one side; species protection and welfare on the other.
source: Britannica; NOAA Fisheries Makah chronology; IWC aboriginal-subsistence records; Faroese grindadrap coverage
framing_note: CONTESTED, both sides, no verdict, vision_mandated. Cultural/treaty rights vs. species protection, each in its strongest honest form. Named handles (Makah 1999, grindadrap, umialik) as answers. Present the hunts factually; do not cast either side as villains.

name: The Atlatl
scope: The spear-thrower that predated the bow by tens of thousands of years. A flick of the wrist launches a 5-foot dart at 80-90 mph; the lever effectively lengthens the throwing arm and adds up to ~60% more force. Ice Age hunters brought down mammoths with it; it survived in the Aztec 'atlatl' (the word we still use) and the Australian woomera. A hook or spur at the end cradles the dart's base.
source: Britannica; Nature Scientific Reports (Bebber et al. 2023, atlatl velocity study); World Atlatl Association
framing_note: Scene-led wonder: the hunter's arm made longer by a stick of antler. Hunting as ancient human skill (30,000+ yrs), presented with respect, no advocacy. Answer = the named tool (atlatl/woomera) or the vivid payoff (dart at highway speed), never a bare date.

name: The Bow and Arrow's Deep Origins
scope: Stone points from Sibudu Cave, South Africa, push arrow-hunting back ~64,000 years — long before it reached Europe. The bow stores elastic energy in the stave itself; it let one hunter carry many light, fast shots. The self bow (one piece of yew, the English longbow) versus the composite recurve (horn, wood, and sinew glued in layers, the steppe horseman's weapon). It eventually displaced the atlatl in much of the world.
source: Britannica; Backwell & d'Errico Sibudu Cave research; longbow/composite-bow histories
framing_note: Wonder at how old this technology is (older than farming, writing, cities). Named place (Sibudu Cave) and named bow types (longbow, composite recurve) as memorable handles. Hunting legitimate and ancient; no advocacy.

name: The Buffalo Jump
scope: Plains nations stampeded whole bison herds off a cliff — Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump in Alberta, used for nearly 6,000 years, its name from a boy said to have watched from under the ledge and been crushed. Runners disguised in wolf and buffalo skins funneled the herd along stone drive lanes. Below the cliff, a bone bed 10 meters deep records the kills; a single drive could feed a band for a winter.
source: Britannica; UNESCO World Heritage (Head-Smashed-In, inscribed 1981); Parks Canada; Blackfoot oral history
framing_note: Scene-led: the disguised runner, the thundering herd, the named cliff, the deep bone bed. Communal Indigenous hunting shown with weight and skill, no-waste ethic implicit (whole herd butchered). No advocacy.

name: Yankee Whaling and the Sperm Whale
scope: Nantucket and New Bedford fleets chased the sperm whale across every ocean in the 1700s-1800s on voyages that lasted years. In its huge blunt head sat spermaceti, a waxy oil that made the finest, cleanest-burning smokeless candles; a struck whale might tow the boat in a 'Nantucket sleigh ride' or smash it to splinters (the whaleship Essex was rammed and sunk by a sperm whale in 1820, giving Melville his 'Moby-Dick'). Grey lumps of ambergris coughed from the gut fixed the perfumes of Europe.
source: Britannica; Nathaniel Philbrick, 'In the Heart of the Sea'; New Bedford Whaling Museum
framing_note: Scene-led wonder: the harpoon, the 'Nantucket sleigh ride,' the whale that sank the Essex, the try-pots rendering blubber on deck. Named things (spermaceti, ambergris, Essex, Moby-Dick) as answers. Historical practice told with wonder, no advocacy.

name: The Chinese Dragon: Rain-Bringer, Not Monster
scope: The Chinese dragon (long) is a benevolent water-and-sky spirit that brings rain and prosperity — the opposite of the fire-breathing Western villain; it has the body of nine animals, the emperor sat on the 'Dragon Throne,' and only he could wear the five-clawed dragon.
source: Britannica: Chinese dragon (long); imperial iconography
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, symmetric respect. Answer = the Chinese dragon, or the vivid contrast (a good luck-bringing rain dragon vs. the Western evil dragon; the emperor's five-clawed monopoly). The nine-animal composite is a concrete handle.

name: The Chinese Zodiac and the Great Race
scope: The twelve animals — Rat, Ox, Tiger, Rabbit, Dragon, Snake, Horse, Goat, Monkey, Rooster, Dog, Pig — and the Jade Emperor's river race that set their order: the clever Rat rode the Ox's head and leapt off at the finish to win, and the Cat was cheated out of a place (some say the Rat never woke it).
source: Britannica: Chinese zodiac (shengxiao); traditional race legend
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition presented straight. Answer = the named animal or the vivid trick (the rat riding then leaping off the ox to win; why the cat is missing). Deep ladder: race order at low tiers, individual animals' traits and the missing-cat mystery deeper. No rote 'list the zodiac' — always via story.

name: The Lamb of God and the Agnus Dei
scope: Christ as the sacrificial lamb: John the Baptist calls Jesus 'the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world,' fulfilling the Passover lamb whose blood spared the Israelites; the Agnus Dei image shows a lamb bearing a banner of victory.
source: Britannica: Agnus Dei; Gospel of John 1:29; Exodus (Passover)
framing_note: Scene-led, Christian tradition presented straight and on the same plane as the others — no privileging, no slighting. Answer = the Lamb of God, or the vivid link (the Passover lamb's blood fulfilled in Christ). Keep the symbol concrete.

name: Anubis, the Jackal Who Weighs Your Heart
scope: The black jackal-headed god who embalmed the dead and stood at the scales in the Hall of Judgment; the dead person's heart weighed against the feather of Ma'at, and if it was heavier, the monster Ammit devoured it. Anubis invented mummification when he wrapped Osiris.
source: Britannica: Anubis; Pinch, Egyptian Mythology (Handbook of the Gods)
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, Egyptian tradition presented straight and seriously. Answer = the named god (Anubis) or the vivid act (the heart weighed against a feather; Ammit waiting to devour). The scales-of-judgment image is the Dinner-Test hook; the black-jackal-as-embalmer is the concrete handle.

name: Balto and Togo: The 1925 Serum Run to Nome
scope: When diphtheria threatened Nome, Alaska in 1925, teams of sled dogs relayed lifesaving serum across ~674 miles of blizzard; Togo, Leonhard Seppala's lead dog, ran by far the longest and most dangerous leg, while Balto, who ran the short final stretch into Nome, got the statue in New York and the fame.
source: Britannica: 1925 serum run to Nome; contemporary accounts of Togo and Balto
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight. Answer = the named dog (Togo did the hardest leg; Balto got the fame) or the vivid relay (sled dogs racing serum through a blizzard to a dying town). The Togo-did-the-work / Balto-got-the-glory contrast is the payoff.

name: Bucephalus, the Horse Only Alexander Could Tame
scope: The great black stallion no one could ride until the boy Alexander noticed the horse was terrified of its own shadow, turned it to face the sun, and mounted it; Bucephalus carried him across an empire to India, and Alexander founded a city, Bucephala, in the horse's memory when it died.
source: Britannica: Bucephalus; Plutarch, Life of Alexander; Arrian, Anabasis
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story told straight. Answer = Bucephalus, or the vivid insight (a boy spotting that the wild horse feared its own shadow). The city named for the horse is the T4 payoff.

name: Cher Ami, the Pigeon Who Saved the Lost Battalion
scope: A carrier pigeon of WWI who, shot through the breast with a leg nearly torn off, flew ~25 miles in about 25 minutes carrying the message that stopped friendly artillery from shelling the trapped 'Lost Battalion'; 194 of the surrounded men survived. Cher Ami earned the Croix de Guerre and is preserved at the Smithsonian.
source: Britannica: Cher Ami; Smithsonian National Museum of American History
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight. Answer = Cher Ami, or the vivid flight (a gravely wounded pigeon flying the message that saved the surrounded battalion). Note the lost-leg and message as documented; treat the popular 'lost an eye' detail cautiously (photos dispute it) — don't assert it as fact.

name: Hachiko, the Dog Who Waited Nine Years
scope: The Akita who met his professor every evening at Tokyo's Shibuya Station — and, after the professor died suddenly at work in 1925, returned to the same spot at the same time each day for nine more years until his own death. A bronze statue of him stands at Shibuya today.
source: Britannica: Hachiko; contemporary Japanese newspaper accounts; Shibuya statue
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight, emotionally plain (no over-anthropomorphizing beyond the documented waiting). Answer = Hachiko, or the vivid fact (nine years of waiting at the same station for a man who would never come). The bronze statue is the T3 handle.

name: Hannibal's War Elephants Over the Alps
scope: In 218 BC Hannibal marched ~37 war elephants across the freezing Alps to invade Italy; most died on the crossing or soon after, but the few survivors terrified Roman soldiers and horses who had never seen such beasts. One elephant, Surus, was said to be his favorite.
source: Britannica: Hannibal; Polybius, Histories; Livy, Ab Urbe Condita
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight. Answer = the war elephants over the Alps, or the vivid image (elephants freezing on a mountain pass to terrify Rome). Keep the animal central, not the campaign logistics.

name: Laika, the First Living Being in Orbit
scope: A gentle Moscow street dog chosen by the Soviets for Sputnik 2 in November 1957, becoming the first animal to orbit Earth; the capsule had no way to return her, and she died of overheating within hours — a fact only fully admitted decades later.
source: Britannica: Laika; Soviet space program records; later Russian disclosures
framing_note: Scene-led, true story straight and honest (including the one-way nature and the later admission). Answer = Laika, or the vivid fact (a street dog became the first creature to orbit Earth, with no way home). Handle the death factually and soberly, not sentimentally.

name: Sergeant Stubby, the Most Decorated Dog of WWI
scope: A stray Boston terrier mix smuggled to the trenches of France, Stubby learned to warn his unit of gas attacks by smell before the men could sense it, found wounded soldiers in no-man's-land, and once held a German infiltrator by the seat of his pants until help came — earning him a sergeant's rank.
source: Britannica: Sergeant Stubby; Smithsonian National Museum of American History
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight. Answer = Stubby, or the vivid deed (smelling gas before the men could; catching a spy by the trousers). The gas-warning and spy-capture are the Dinner-Test payoffs.

name: Wojtek, the Bear Who Carried Shells at Monte Cassino
scope: A Syrian brown bear cub bought from a boy in Iran and raised by Polish soldiers, who officially enlisted him as a private (later corporal) in the 22nd Artillery Supply Company so he could travel by troopship; at Monte Cassino in 1944 he carried heavy crates of artillery shells and never dropped one. He retired to Edinburgh Zoo.
source: Britannica: Wojtek the Bear; Imperial War Museum accounts
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight. Answer = Wojtek, or the vivid fact (an enlisted bear who hauled artillery shells in battle). The 22nd Company adopted a bear-carrying-a-shell as its emblem — a great handle.

name: Pegasus, the Winged Horse Born of Blood
scope: The white winged horse who sprang from Medusa's neck when Perseus beheaded her; the hero Bellerophon tamed him with Athena's golden bridle and rode him to slay the fire-breathing Chimera, then was thrown when he tried to fly to Olympus. Pegasus became a constellation.
source: Britannica: Pegasus; Hesiod, Theogony; Apollodorus, Library
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the named creature (Pegasus) or the vivid origin (born from Medusa's severed neck). Bellerophon's fall for overreaching is the memorable moral beat. Keep names as context, not 'who rode Pegasus' cold trivia.

name: Ganesha, the Elephant-Headed Remover of Obstacles
scope: The elephant-headed god of beginnings and remover of obstacles; his father Shiva beheaded him not recognizing him and replaced the head with an elephant's; he rides a tiny mouse, and broke off his own tusk to use as a pen to write down the Mahabharata.
source: Britannica: Ganesha; the Puranas; the Mahabharata frame-story
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight. Answer = Ganesha, or the vivid detail (elephant head on a boy's body; an elephant god who rides a mouse; the tusk-pen). The mismatched mount and the broken tusk are the Dinner-Test payoffs.

name: Hanuman, the Monkey God Who Leapt to Lanka
scope: The mighty monkey (vanara) devotee of Rama who leapt across the ocean to Lanka to find the captive Sita, and when told to fetch one healing herb, carried back the entire mountain because he couldn't tell which plant it was. The model of selfless devotion.
source: Britannica: Hanuman; Valmiki, Ramayana
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition presented straight and reverently. Answer = Hanuman, or the vivid feat (leaping the sea; carrying a whole mountain to be sure of the healing herb). Devotion is the emotional spine; keep it wondrous, not doctrinal.

name: Fenrir, the Wolf Chained Until Ragnarok
scope: Loki's monstrous wolf-son who grew so fast the gods feared him; they bound him with the impossibly-soft magic ribbon Gleipnir made of six impossible things, but only after Tyr placed his hand in Fenrir's jaws as a pledge — and lost it. At Ragnarok, Fenrir breaks free and swallows Odin.
source: Britannica: Fenrir; Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda (Gylfaginning)
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = Fenrir, or the vivid sacrifice (Tyr gave his hand into the wolf's mouth so the gods could chain it). The soft ribbon made of impossible things and the doom of swallowing Odin are the deep-tier payoffs.

name: Huginn and Muninn, Odin's Spy Ravens
scope: The two ravens 'Thought' and 'Memory' who fly across the whole world every dawn and return to whisper the news into Odin's ears; Odin admits he fears more for Muninn (Memory) not coming back. Ravens circling a battlefield were seen as Odin's own.
source: Britannica: Huginn and Muninn; Poetic Edda (Grimnismal); Snorri, Prose Edda
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the named ravens (Huginn and Muninn / Thought and Memory) or the vivid act (they fly the world daily and report back). Odin fearing to lose Memory is the poignant beat.

name: Jormungandr, the World Serpent
scope: Loki's serpent-child, flung into the ocean, grew so vast it circles the whole world and bites its own tail; Thor once hooked it while fishing with an ox-head bait and nearly hauled it up. At Ragnarok, Thor kills it but dies from its venom after nine steps.
source: Britannica: Jormungandr; Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda; Poetic Edda (Hymiskvida)
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = Jormungandr (the World Serpent) or the vivid image (a snake so huge it wraps the world biting its tail; Thor fishing for it). Thor's mutual doom with the serpent is the T4 beat.

name: Sleipnir, Odin's Eight-Legged Horse
scope: The gray eight-legged steed who carried Odin across the sky and down to the land of the dead; born when Loki, disguised as a mare, lured away the giant builder's stallion Svadilfari — making Loki the horse's mother. The fastest horse in the Nine Worlds.
source: Britannica: Sleipnir; Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda (Gylfaginning)
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = Sleipnir, or the vivid origin (Loki turned into a mare and gave birth to Odin's horse). Eight legs and the shapeshifting birth are the Dinner-Test payoffs.

name: The Monarch Butterfly's Migration
scope: Every autumn monarchs stream up to 3,000 miles from Canada and the US to a few mountain forests in Mexico — but no single butterfly makes the round trip. It takes three to four generations to return north, so the butterflies arriving at the exact same overwintering trees have never been there, navigating by an inherited sun-compass.
source: Britannica; Monarch Watch; Reppert lab (sun-compass navigation)
framing_note: The 'great-great-grandchildren return to a place they've never seen' paradox is the hook. Scene-led. State the multi-generational fact accurately. Cross-refs monarch toxicity (defense ladder) but stays about migration here.

name: A Dog's Nose (dog olfaction)
scope: A dog smells a world we can't imagine: roughly 300 million scent receptors to a human's 6 million, and a slice of brain devoted to smell about 40 times larger relatively. A trained dog can detect a teaspoon of sugar diluted in two Olympic swimming pools, and reads time by how a scent has faded.
source: Britannica; Alexandra Horowitz 'Being a Dog'; canine olfaction literature
framing_note: The scale comparisons (two swimming pools; smelling the passage of time) are the payoffs — number as constructed punchline, not cold stat. Scene-led. Ties forward to Pillar 3 detection dogs but stays about the biology here.

name: What Makes a Bird
scope: Feathers (the one trait no other living animal has), toothless beaks, hard-shelled eggs, warm blood, and air-filled hollow bones that make flight possible. Payoff: feathers evolved before flight, and birds descend from theropod dinosaurs.
source: Britannica; Cornell Lab of Ornithology; AMNH
framing_note: Feathers = the defining tell (leads every rung). Scene-led, not 'define bird.' Dinosaur ancestry stated as standard biology.

name: What Makes a Mammal
scope: The three hidden signatures every mammal shares: milk (mammary glands, the name-giving trait), hair/fur, and three tiny middle-ear bones (malleus, incus, stapes) that no other animal has. Warm-blooded and mostly live-bearing. Payoff rung: those three ear bones started as reptile jaw bones.
source: Britannica; AMNH; UCMP Berkeley
framing_note: Scene-led: the surprise is the three-ear-bones signature (invisible from outside, unique to mammals). Concrete handle over jargon; keep the jaw-bone-to-ear-bone evolution factual and plain, no theology.

name: The Peregrine Falcon's Dive
scope: The fastest animal on Earth is not a runner but a diver: a peregrine falcon in a hunting stoop exceeds 300 km/h (about 240 mph), fast enough that little cones of bone in its nostrils are thought to keep the rushing air from bursting its lungs, and a special third eyelid wipes the eye clear mid-dive.
source: Britannica; peregrine stoop aerodynamics; falcon nostril-cone hypothesis
framing_note: The 240-mph dive and the nostril-cones-so-its-lungs-don't-burst fact are the payoffs. Scene-led. Accuracy: 'fastest animal' = in a dive specifically; the nostril-cone role is a well-cited hypothesis - frame accordingly.

name: The Pistol Shrimp's Snap
scope: A shrimp barely 2 inches long snaps its oversized claw so fast it fires a bubble bullet — a collapsing cavitation bubble that momentarily reaches roughly 4,700°C (nearly the surface temperature of the sun) and stuns prey with the shockwave, not the claw itself. Colonies snapping together are loud enough to disrupt sonar.
source: Versluis et al. 2000 (snapping shrimp cavitation & sonoluminescence, Science); Britannica
framing_note: The 'as hot as the sun's surface for an instant' comparison is the payoff (number constructed as punchline). Accuracy: the heat is brief and localized in the collapsing bubble. Scene-led. Distinct from mantis shrimp (different animal, different mechanism).

name: Tiktaalik, the Fishapod
scope: Neil Shubin bet evolution was predictable: he searched 375-million-year-old Devonian rock on Ellesmere Island because that was where and when a fish-to-land transitional SHOULD be — and in 2004 found Tiktaalik, a fish with a neck, wrists, and proto-limbs.
source: Shubin, Your Inner Fish; UChicago Biological Sciences; Nature 2006; Tiktaalik.uchicago.edu
framing_note: The prediction is the wow — Shubin picked the rock's age and place, then the fossil showed up. Standard science stated confidently. Discovered 2004, published 2006, ~375M; answer is the NAMED fishapod and the successful prediction, not a date.

name: Human Evolution Is a Bush, Not a Ladder
scope: The famous 'march of progress' image is wrong — human evolution isn't a straight line from ape to us. Multiple human species lived AT THE SAME TIME: as recently as ~50,000 years ago, Homo sapiens, Neanderthals, Denisovans, and the tiny 'hobbit' Homo floresiensis shared the planet. It's a branching bush, not a ladder.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Homo floresiensis literature; Gould on the bush metaphor
framing_note: NAME the misconception explicitly (the straight-line 'march of progress'). The 'four human species coexisted, including a hobbit' payoff. Standard science stated confidently. The bush-vs-ladder concept is the answer, not a date.

name: Birds ARE Dinosaurs
scope: The chickadee at the feeder is a living theropod dinosaur — the wishbone, hollow bones, three-fingered hand, feathers, and a special half-moon wrist bone (the semilunate carpal) that let raptors fold their arms are all inherited straight from dinosaurs; dinosaurs never fully went extinct.
source: Britannica; NHM London; theropod-bird phylogeny literature
framing_note: The 'dinosaurs are still alive at your bird feeder' payoff is core wonder. Standard science stated confidently and plainly — not hedged. Concrete shared traits (wishbone, semilunate wrist) as handles.

name: Pleistocene Overkill vs. Climate
scope: Why did the mammoths, sabertooths, and giant sloths vanish ~13,000-10,000 years ago? Paul Martin's 1967 'overkill' hypothesis blames human hunters arriving and wiping them out fast; the rival view blames abrupt climate change at the Ice Age's end. Scientists still argue, and the answer likely differs by continent.
source: Paul Martin 1967 overkill; Britannica; late-Quaternary extinction debate literature (Barnosky, Koch & Barnosky)
framing_note: THE contested paleo topic — present BOTH sides fully and fairly, NO verdict. Attribute overkill to Paul Martin 1967; give the climate hypothesis equal, non-dismissive weight ('the overkill hypothesis argues...' vs '...misguidedly believe'). Wonder-led, not advocacy.

name: The Permian Great Dying
scope: 252M years ago Siberian Traps volcanism cooked the planet and killed ~95% of all marine species and ~70% of land species — life came within a whisker of ending; the closest Earth ever came to a lifeless ocean.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Siberian Traps / end-Permian literature
framing_note: Build the stem toward the 95% payoff so the number LANDS as a gut-punch (constructed, not cold). Standard science; name the Siberian Traps as cause. 'The Great Dying' is a legitimate named-thing answer.

name: Angus: The Black Polled Scot
scope: Aberdeen Angus (Scotland; solid black; naturally polled/hornless; most popular US beef breed; the 'Certified Angus Beef' brand and its grading spec); why the polled gene matters for handling and dehorning; the marbling reputation; Red Angus as the recessive-color offshoot.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; American Angus Association; Certified Angus Beef; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the black, hornless Scottish breed behind most American beef' → Angus. Named breed + trait (polled, black), never 'what is a beef breed?'. No policy drift.

name: Holstein: The Milk Champion
scope: Holstein-Friesian (black-and-white from Friesland/Holland; the dairy volume champion at ~10,000+ gal/cow/year; ~90% of US dairy cattle); the unique black-and-white spotting used as ID; why sheer volume (not richness) made it the industrial dairy standard; the red-and-white recessive variant.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; Holstein Association USA; USDA dairy statistics; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the black-and-white Friesian, the world's milk champion' → Holstein. Named breed + the volume record. No policy drift.

name: Jersey & Channel-Island Dairy
scope: Jersey (small fawn-colored Channel Islands breed; highest butterfat in milk; gentle temperament; efficient feed-to-milk on smaller frame); Guernsey (larger, golden 'Golden Guernsey' milk high in beta-carotene); why butterfat drives cheese and cream yield; the island herd-book purity laws.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; American Jersey Cattle Association; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the small fawn Channel Islands cow whose milk carries the highest butterfat' → Jersey. Named breed + butterfat trait, never a bare definition. No policy drift.

name: Wagyu, Kobe & Marbling
scope: Wagyu = the Japanese breed group (literally 'Japanese cattle'), Kobe = a protected brand of Tajima-strain Wagyu from Hyogo Prefecture only; intramuscular fat marbling (the BMS score 1-12); the four Wagyu strains (Japanese Black dominant); why 'Kobe beef' outside Hyogo is usually mislabeled; monounsaturated-fat melting point.
source: Britannica; Kobe Beef Marketing & Distribution Promotion Association; Japan Meat Grading Association
framing_note: Scene-led: the marbled Tajima steer of Hyogo. The Wagyu-is-the-breed / Kobe-is-the-brand distinction is the load-bearing reveal. No policy drift.

name: CAFOs: Concerns & Tradeoffs
scope: Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations — the scale that made meat cheap; real concerns (manure lagoons and nutrient runoff, routine antibiotic use and resistance, confinement welfare, air quality, disease spread) set against the genuine cost / food-access tradeoff (industrial husbandry feeds billions affordably); why 'done well or poorly' matters more than the format alone.
source: EPA CAFO definitions; Pew Commission on Industrial Farm Animal Production; USDA data
framing_note: CONTESTED with a firm floor: cruelty is wrong (state that plainly), AND the cheap-food/access tradeoff is real — present the runoff/antibiotic/welfare concerns and the affordability case as a genuine debate, no verdict on the system itself. Scene-led on the lagoon and the feed bunk. No legislative/policy drift.

name: The Five Freedoms (Brambell 1965)
scope: The 1965 Brambell Report (UK response to Ruth Harrison's 'Animal Machines') and the Farm Animal Welfare Council's Five Freedoms: freedom from hunger/thirst; from discomfort; from pain/injury/disease; to express normal behavior; from fear and distress; how this became the global welfare baseline; the newer 'Five Domains' successor that adds positive mental states.
source: Brambell Report 1965; UK Farm Animal Welfare Council; Mellor (2016) Five Domains
framing_note: HUMANE-TREATMENT stance FIRM: the Five Freedoms are real and matter — present them as a genuine, load-bearing standard, not one 'view'. Scene-led: Ruth Harrison's book that shamed a government into acting. No policy drift beyond the framework itself.

name: Fair Chase
scope: The core ethic of sport hunting: the animal must have a genuine chance to escape, so the hunt is a test of skill, not a slaughter. It rules out shooting a tame or fenced-in animal (a 'canned hunt'), using spotlights, running game with vehicles or aircraft, or shooting an animal in water. The Boone and Crockett Club, founded by Theodore Roosevelt and George Bird Grinnell in 1887, wrote the standard down.
source: Britannica; Boone and Crockett Club fair-chase statement; hunter-ethics literature
framing_note: vision_mandated: this carries the bank's hunting stance. Present fair chase as the actual principle hunters hold — legitimate, no advocacy either way. The canned-hunt contrast makes it concrete. Named body (Boone and Crockett) as context, not a memorize-the-founding-date rung.

name: No Waste
scope: Across hunting cultures runs one rule: take only what you will use, and use what you take. Wanton waste — killing for the antlers and leaving the meat, or the hide-hunters who let bison carcasses rot — is the cardinal sin. Many states make wanton waste of edible game meat a crime, and traditional cultures wove thanks and use-it-all customs around the kill.
source: Britannica; state game-law waste provisions; Indigenous and hunter-ethics traditions
framing_note: vision_mandated stance topic. The no-waste ethic tied back to the bison-slaughter and nose-to-tail ladders. Present as the shared principle, legitimate hunting, no advocacy. Keep the emphasis on the ETHIC and the animal, not on statute text.

name: The Quick, Clean Kill
scope: The ethical hunter's obligation is to kill fast and minimize suffering: knowing the vital zone (the heart-lung 'boiler room' behind the shoulder), choosing a weapon and load equal to the animal, staying inside one's effective range, and passing on a bad or marginal shot. A wounded animal that runs off must be tracked and recovered, not abandoned — the blood trail is followed to the end.
source: Britannica; hunter-education curricula; ethical-hunting literature
framing_note: vision_mandated stance topic + directly practical (shot placement is the player's kill quality). Present as the real skill and duty hunters practice, not as advocacy. The tracking-the-wounded duty is the moral weight. No preaching either direction.

name: The Trophy Hunting Debate
scope: Whether killing a lion or elephant for a trophy can be good for the species. In some African programs — Zimbabwe's CAMPFIRE — high-priced hunts have funded rural communities and given them a reason to protect wildlife and habitat rather than clear it for cattle, and Zimbabwe holds Africa's second-largest elephant herd. Critics answer that it is ethically repugnant, that corruption siphons much of the money before it reaches villages, and that killing prime breeding males (the 2015 Cecil the lion case) harms the pride and the gene pool.
source: Britannica; CAMPFIRE Association Zimbabwe; IUCN sustainable-use briefings; Cecil-the-lion coverage
framing_note: CONTESTED, both sides, no verdict, vision_mandated. State the conservation-funding case (CAMPFIRE, the elephant numbers, incentive-to-protect) AND the ethical + corruption + prime-male critique, each fairly. Named handles (CAMPFIRE, Cecil) as answers. Present, don't preach.

name: The Pre-Stunning Debate
scope: Modern slaughterhouses stun an animal senseless before the cut (captive-bolt, electric, or gas); the EU and UK generally require it on welfare grounds. Some Jewish and Muslim authorities hold that the animal must be uninjured and alive at the cut, and seek a religious-freedom exemption from stunning. Others within those communities accept certain reversible stuns, or argue that a well-made cut with a razor-sharp blade is itself humane. The two goods — animal welfare and religious liberty — are in real tension.
source: Britannica; EU/UK slaughter-welfare regulation debates; RSPCA and religious-community position papers
framing_note: CONTESTED, both sides, no verdict, vision_mandated. Frame it as welfare vs. religious liberty, each stated in its strongest honest form — no side cast as villains, and note the internal disagreement within faith communities. Present, don't preach.

name: Bastet, the Cat Goddess of Bubastis
scope: The goddess of home, protection, and cats, worshipped at Bubastis; began as a fierce lioness and softened into a cat over centuries; her festival drew huge river-boat crowds (Herodotus). Cats were so sacred that harming one could be a capital crime.
source: Britannica: Bastet; Herodotus, Histories II; Pinch, Egyptian Mythology
framing_note: Scene-led, symmetric respect. Answer = the named goddess (Bastet) or the vivid turn (a lioness who became a house cat; killing a cat could cost a life). Keep it wondrous, not smug about 'cat worship.'

name: The Giraffe's Impossible Neck
scope: The tallest animal solves problems its height creates: a heart about 60 cm long pumps at roughly double human blood pressure to reach the brain two metres up, tight leg skin acts like a pilot's g-suit to stop blood pooling, and special valves keep it from blacking out when it swings its head down to drink. Its neck has just seven bones - the same number as a human.
source: Britannica; giraffe cardiovascular physiology literature
framing_note: The double-blood-pressure heart, the g-suit legs, and the same-seven-neck-bones-as-a-human facts are the payoffs. Scene-led. Numbers built as punchlines. Factual anatomy.

name: The Platypus, Head to Tail
scope: Beyond laying eggs, the platypus is a walking checklist of oddities: a leathery duck bill that reads electric fields underwater, webbed feet, a beaver-like tail that stores fat, venomous ankle spurs on the males, and - under UV light - fur that glows biofluorescent green-blue, a trait discovered only in 2020.
source: Britannica; Australian Museum; Anich et al. 2020 (platypus biofluorescence, Mammalia)
framing_note: A deeper companion to the monotreme ladder, focused on the platypus's stacked oddities (venom spur, electro-bill, 2020 glow-in-UV discovery). Real binomial Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Scene-led. Factual, no anthropomorphizing.

name: Late & Regional Domesticates
scope: The reindeer as the most recent large-animal domesticate (~2,000 BP, Siberian Sami and others, half-wild herding); the llama and alpaca (Andean, from guanaco and vicuna, ~5,000 BP, cargo + fiber); the water buffalo, yak, bactrian camel and dromedary as regional workhorses; the guinea pig and turkey as New World domesticates.
source: Britannica; FAO domestic-animal-diversity; Andean camelid domestication literature
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the most recent large-animal domesticate, still half-wild on the Siberian tundra' → reindeer; 'the Andean cargo animal bred from the wild guanaco' → llama. Named animal + region. No policy drift.

name: Heritage & Acorn-Fed Pigs
scope: Berkshire (English heritage, black with six white points, prized 'Kurobuta' pork); Tamworth (Irish/English, ginger-red, the classic bacon pig); Iberico of the Spanish dehesa (Pata Negra; Bellota grade acorn-finished for jamon iberico); Mangalitsa (Hungarian curly 'wooly pig', near-extinct then restored, extreme lard marbling); Gloucestershire Old Spots; why acorn/pannage finishing changes the fat.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; Britannica; Fundacion del Jamon Iberico; Mangalica breeders
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the curly-coated Hungarian wooly pig' → Mangalitsa; 'the black-hoofed pig fattened on dehesa acorns for jamon' → Iberico. Acorn-finishing is the memorable practical hook (fat quality). No policy drift.

name: Charcuterie — Curing the Whole Animal
scope: The old arts of preserving meat: prosciutto di Parma (a pork leg salted and air-dried a year or more, no smoke), Spanish jamon Iberico de bellota from acorn-fed black-hoofed pigs, salami and the white 'good mold' on its skin, mortadella studded with fat cubes, blood sausage (boudin noir), and headcheese set into a terrine from the meat of a boiled head. Salt, time, nitrate, and controlled mold turn fresh meat into something that keeps for months without refrigeration.
source: Britannica; 'Charcuterie' (Ruhlman & Polcyn); Italian/Spanish DOP records
framing_note: Practical + wonder: preserving the whole animal is real harvest skill and delicious lore. Named products (prosciutto, jamon Iberico, mortadella, boudin noir) as answers. Ties to no-waste. No stance issues.

name: Kosher Slaughter — Shechita
scope: A trained shochet uses the chalaf — a blade so smooth and sharp it must be checked for the tiniest nick against a fingernail — to sever the trachea, esophagus, both carotid arteries, and the jugular in one uninterrupted stroke, intended to be swift and to drain the blood (Torah forbids consuming blood; meat is later salted to draw out any remaining). Only certain animals qualify (cud-chewing split-hoofed, so no pork), the carcass is inspected, and a lung adhesion can make it non-kosher (treif) while a flawless one is glatt. Meat and dairy stay separate.
source: Britannica; Jewish Virtual Library; OU Kosher references
framing_note: Present the practice respectfully and precisely as its practitioners understand it (swift single cut, blood prohibition, salting, glatt). Named terms (shochet, chalaf, glatt, treif) as answers with context. Neutral, factual, no verdict on the practice. No advocacy.

name: The Inuit Seal Hunt and Harpoon
scope: The toggling harpoon head turns sideways inside the seal so it cannot pull free; a sealskin float (avataq) tires the animal and keeps it from sinking. The hunter waits motionless at the seal's breathing hole (aglu) in the sea ice for hours, sometimes with a feather set to twitch at the first breath. Sealskin sewn with sinew made the only truly waterproof clothing in the Arctic; the catch was shared by custom across the camp.
source: Britannica; Canadian Museum of History; Smithsonian Arctic Studies Center
framing_note: Wonder at ingenious cold-adapted technology (toggling head, float, waterproof gut parkas, breathing-hole wait). Indigenous subsistence hunting shown as legitimate and skilled; sharing custom highlights no-waste. No advocacy.

name: The Peacock and the Pelican: Medieval Christian Beasts
scope: The peacock, whose flesh was believed never to rot, stood for resurrection and its hundred-eyed tail for an all-seeing God; the pelican, believed to pierce its own breast to feed its young with its blood, became a symbol of Christ's self-sacrifice. Both from the medieval bestiaries.
source: Britannica: bestiary; medieval Physiologus tradition
framing_note: Scene-led, tradition straight, same plane. Answer = the named bird and its meaning (peacock = incorruptible resurrection; pelican = self-sacrifice). The 'flesh that never rots' and the self-wounding pelican are the Dinner-Test payoffs, presented as the belief held (bestiary lore), not as fact.

name: Falconry: The Feathered Rank of Kings
scope: The ancient art of hunting with trained birds of prey, named a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage; in the medieval 'Boke of St Albans' a strict pecking order matched bird to rank — an eagle for an emperor, a gyrfalcon for a king, a peregrine for a prince, down to a kestrel for a servant.
source: Britannica: falconry; the Boke of St Albans; UNESCO Intangible Heritage listing
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = falconry / the named bird-to-rank match (the king's gyrfalcon), or the vivid fact (a medieval law of which bird your rank could fly). The rank-by-raptor table is a great Dinner-Test hook.

name: The Buffalo, Center of Plains Life
scope: The American bison was the whole economy and spirit of the Plains nations — meat, hide for tipis and robes, sinew for thread, bone for tools, and a sacred being honored in the White Buffalo Calf Woman story of the Lakota, who brought the sacred pipe.
source: Britannica: bison and Plains cultures; Lakota White Buffalo Calf Woman tradition
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight. Answer = the buffalo/bison, or the vivid use (nearly every part of the animal became food, shelter, or tool) and the White Buffalo Calf Woman story. Keep the reverence and the near-total use central; the population collapse belongs to Pillar 4, so keep the animal-in-culture the focus here.

name: Mongol Horse Archers: An Empire on Horseback
scope: The Mongol warrior's bond with the small tough steppe horse — each rider led three to five remounts so he could ride for days, drank fermented mare's milk (airag), and could loose arrows accurately at a gallop by shooting in the instant all four hooves left the ground.
source: Britannica: Mongol military; steppe cavalry history
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, told straight. Answer = the Mongol horse / horse archer, or the vivid technique (firing arrows in the split second all four hooves are off the ground; multiple remounts giving unmatched range). Keep the horse-and-rider partnership central.

name: Colonies That Act Like One Animal (eusociality)
scope: In a few animals, most individuals give up breeding to serve one queen and raise her young — the whole colony works like a single body. Ants, honeybees, and termites do it, and so, uniquely among mammals, does the naked mole-rat. A single leafcutter-ant colony can farm fungus and number millions.
source: Britannica; E.O. Wilson 'The Insect Societies'; leafcutter ant biology
framing_note: The 'colony as one super-organism' idea and the mammal exception (naked mole-rat) are the hooks. Teach eusociality after the concrete example. Scene-led. Cross-refs the mole-rat ladder.

name: Crows That Make Tools
scope: New Caledonian crows don't just use sticks — they manufacture tools, snipping and shaping hooked twigs and barbed leaf-edges to fish grubs out of holes, and they pass techniques to their young. In lab tests one crow, Betty, bent a straight wire into a hook to lift a bucket, and crows solve multi-step puzzles like the fable of the crow and the pitcher.
source: Britannica; Alex Kacelnik / Oxford (Betty the crow); Gavin Hunt (tool manufacture)
framing_note: The 'bent a wire into a hook, unprompted' and 'passes Aesop's pitcher test' facts are payoffs. Scene-led. Present as documented problem-solving, not human-level thought. Cross-refs crow_intelligence in the cognition strand; keep this about tool-making.

name: Elephants and Their Dead
scope: Elephants react to death unlike almost any other animal: herds have been documented stopping to investigate the bones and tusks of dead elephants — touching and turning them gently with trunks and feet, and lingering — grief-like behavior that researchers study carefully without claiming to know the animal's inner experience.
source: Britannica; Cynthia Moss / Amboseli Elephant Research; McComb et al. (responses to remains)
framing_note: MANDATORY caution: describe 'grief-LIKE behavior' and 'documented investigation of remains' — do NOT state 'the elephant mourned/cried' as fact (the doc's headline anti-pattern). The restraint IS the honest wonder. Scene-led.

name: The Arctic Tern's Pole-to-Pole Flight
scope: The arctic tern makes the longest migration on Earth, flying from Arctic breeding grounds to Antarctic waters and back — a zig-zagging route totaling roughly 44,000 miles (70,000 km) a year. Because it chases endless summer at both poles, this small seabird sees more daylight than any other animal, and over a lifetime flies the distance of several trips to the Moon.
source: Egevang et al. 2010 (geolocator tracking, PNAS); Britannica
framing_note: The 'sees more sunlight than any animal' and 'lifetime = trips to the Moon' comparisons are the payoffs. Scene-led. Numbers built up, not cold. Longest-migration is well established.

name: The Bee's Waggle Dance
scope: A returning honeybee tells the hive where to find flowers by dancing: it waggles in a straight line whose ANGLE (relative to straight up) encodes the direction toward the sun, and whose DURATION encodes the distance. Karl von Frisch cracked this code and won a Nobel Prize — a language of movement, in the dark, on a vertical comb.
source: Karl von Frisch (waggle dance decoding, 1973 Nobel); Britannica
framing_note: The 'a dance that gives GPS coordinates' reveal is the payoff. Scene-led. von Frisch as context (Nobel), not an 'X said Y' stem. State angle=direction, duration=distance accurately.

name: The Salmon's Journey Home
scope: A salmon hatched in a tiny mountain stream swims to the open ocean for years, then finds its way back to the exact same stream to spawn — steering by Earth's magnetic field over the long haul and by the remembered smell of its home water for the final approach. Pacific species spawn once, then die, feeding the whole forest.
source: Britannica; Lohmann (magnetic imprinting); Hasler & Scholz (olfactory homing)
framing_note: The 'smells its way back to its birth stream' fact plus the spawn-then-die twist are the payoffs. Scene-led. State magnetic + olfactory navigation accurately. Ties to husbandry/aquaculture elsewhere but stays wild-behavior here.

name: The Sea Otter's Toolkit
scope: A sea otter carries a favourite rock in a pouch of loose skin under its arm and uses it as an anvil to smash open shellfish on its chest while floating - one of the few tool-using mammals. It has the densest fur of any animal (up to a million hairs per square inch) because, unlike other sea mammals, it has almost no blubber to keep warm.
source: Britannica; Monterey Bay Aquarium; sea otter tool-use & thermoregulation research
framing_note: The rock-anvil-in-an-armpit-pouch tool use and densest-fur-because-no-blubber facts are the payoffs. Scene-led. Numbers (fur density) built as punchline. Factual.

name: The Sloth's Slow Life
scope: The sloth is built for near-zero effort: it digests a leaf over about a month, moves so slowly that green algae grows in its fur (camouflage plus a private garden), and climbs down its tree only about once a week to relieve itself. Hanging upside down, its hair parts the wrong way so rain runs off.
source: Britannica; sloth physiology; sloth-algae-moth symbiosis research
framing_note: The month-long digestion, algae-in-the-fur garden, and weekly bathroom trip are the retell payoffs. Scene-led. Real biology, factual. No anthropomorphizing 'lazy' - it is an energy strategy.

name: Playing Dead (opossum thanatosis)
scope: When a threat is overwhelming, the Virginia opossum doesn't decide to fake death — it involuntarily flops into a comatose state, tongue out, eyes glazed, and oozes a foul green corpse-smelling fluid from glands, becoming so convincingly 'dead' that a predator loses interest. It can stay this way for minutes to hours before snapping out of it.
source: Britannica; thanatosis (tonic immobility) literature
framing_note: The 'it's INVOLUNTARY, not acting' twist plus the corpse-smell detail are the payoffs. Scene-led ('playing possum' is the folk name, thanatosis the term). State it's a reflex, not a choice — accuracy matters here.

name: The Bombardier Beetle's Chemical Cannon
scope: The bombardier beetle mixes chemical weapons on demand: it stores hydroquinone and hydrogen peroxide separately, then combines them in a reaction chamber where enzymes trigger a boiling explosion that blasts out the tail end as a pulsing spray near 100°C (the boiling point of water) — aimed with a swiveling nozzle straight at an attacker's face.
source: Britannica; Eisner & Aneshansley (bombardier beetle spray mechanism, pulsed jet studies)
framing_note: The 'mixes two chemicals to fire a boiling spray from a swiveling nozzle' fact is the payoff. Scene-led. The pulsed-jet, near-100°C mechanism is well studied — state accurately. Concrete over jargon.

name: The Monarch's Poisonous Childhood
scope: Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed — a plant toxic to most animals — and instead of being harmed they store the poison (cardenolides) in their bodies, staying toxic as adult butterflies. Their bright orange-and-black is a billboard warning, and the harmless viceroy butterfly copies the pattern to freeload on the monarch's bad reputation.
source: Britannica; monarch cardenolide sequestration; Batesian/Müllerian mimicry (viceroy)
framing_note: The 'eats poison to become poison, and a copycat exploits it' story is the payoff (and teaches warning coloration + mimicry). Scene-led. Note the viceroy is now considered co-mimic (Müllerian), not purely a harmless fake — keep it accurate.

name: The Pufferfish's Poison
scope: A pufferfish carries tetrodotoxin, a neurotoxin roughly 1,000 times deadlier than cyanide, with no antidote — it paralyzes the muscles while the victim stays conscious. In Japan it's the delicacy fugu, which by law only licensed chefs trained for years may prepare, cutting away the toxic organs; a wrong cut can kill the diner.
source: Britannica; tetrodotoxin toxicology; Japanese fugu licensing
framing_note: The 'more deadly than cyanide, no antidote, and people pay to eat it' tension is the payoff. Scene-led (the licensed fugu chef). Accuracy: puffers acquire TTX via diet/bacteria; state deadliness without recipe detail. Cross-refs cooking bank but the animal biology stays here.

name: The Skunk's Spray
scope: A skunk's warning is real: it aims a spray of sulfur compounds (thiols) from glands under its tail that can hit a target several feet away and be smelled up to a mile off, clinging for days. It gives fair warning first — stamping, hissing, raising its tail — and can even do a handstand (the spotted skunk) before firing.
source: Britannica; skunk chemistry (thiols); spotted skunk handstand behavior
framing_note: The handstand-before-spraying and smellable-a-mile-off facts are the payoffs. Scene-led. Concrete handle ('sulfur compounds / thiols') over pure chemistry jargon. Factual.

name: Jellyfish, Coral, and Anemones (Cnidarians)
scope: The stinging-cell phylum: jellyfish, corals, sea anemones, and hydra, built on radial symmetry with no brain and no bones. Their weapon is the nematocyst — a microscopic harpoon that fires in under a millisecond, one of the fastest movements in all of biology. A coral reef is millions of tiny animals building limestone cities.
source: Britannica; AMNH; NOAA coral reef resources
framing_note: The harpoon-firing nematocyst is the vivid adaptation payoff. Scene-led (a swimmer brushes a tentacle). No 'define cnidarian.' Coral-as-colony-of-animals is a strong reveal rung.

name: The Insect Orders (beetles rule the world)
scope: The big insect orders: Coleoptera (beetles — the largest order of animals on Earth, ~400,000 named species; 'God has an inordinate fondness for beetles'), Lepidoptera (butterflies and moths), Diptera (flies, one pair of wings), Hymenoptera (bees, ants, wasps). Payoff: roughly 1 in every 4 known animal species is a beetle.
source: Britannica; Smithsonian Entomology; Haldane beetle quote
framing_note: The staggering beetle count is the wonder payoff (number built up as a punchline, not a cold stat). The Haldane 'inordinate fondness for beetles' line is a dinner-table hook. Scene-led.

name: The Mollusk Classes (snail, clam, octopus — same phylum?!)
scope: One phylum stretches from a garden snail to a genius octopus: gastropods (snails, slugs — one muscular foot), bivalves (clams, oysters, mussels — two hinged shells, no head), and cephalopods (octopus, squid, cuttlefish, nautilus — 'head-foot,' arms around the mouth). The surprise: an oyster and an octopus are cousins.
source: Britannica; AMNH; MBARI
framing_note: The reveal that a clam and an octopus share a phylum is the hook. Scene-led. Sets up the octopus ladder. Distractors: put a starfish (echinoderm) or barnacle (crustacean) among mollusks.

name: Animals That Change Sex (sequential hermaphrodites)
scope: Clownfish live in a strict hierarchy: all are born male, and when the dominant female dies the biggest male turns into the new female (so in Finding Nemo, Nemo's dad would have become his mom). Many wrasses do the reverse — the dominant female becomes male. Sex is a role that can flip.
source: Britannica; reef-fish biology literature
framing_note: The Finding Nemo clownfish twist is the ultimate dinner-table retell. Scene-led. Present as observed reef biology, plainly, without projecting onto human debates (this is fish life-history, stays neutral biology).

name: Egg-Layers vs Live-Bearers (and eggs that hatch inside)
scope: The basic split: oviparous animals lay eggs (birds, most fish, reptiles), viviparous animals give live birth (most mammals). The twist: ovoviviparous animals like some sharks and snakes grow eggs that hatch inside the mother, so she appears to give live birth without a placenta.
source: Britannica; AMNH
framing_note: The ovoviviparous 'eggs that hatch inside' twist is the memorable rung. Teach the plain distinction first at T2, then the surprise at T3. Scene-led. Distractors swap the three modes.

name: Peacocks, Antlers, and the Cost of Beauty (sexual selection)
